name: Safe Complexion Wafers

card.summary: Arsenic-containing tablets sold in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and eaten to produce a pale, clear complexion and to remove freckles and blemishes.
card.aka: Dr. Campbell's Safe Arsenic Complexion Wafers, arsenic complexion wafers
card.note: Historical product. Arsenic is a poison; ingesting it is associated with documented deaths and chronic poisoning.

quick.overview:
Safe Complexion Wafers were a Victorian-era beauty product: small tablets containing arsenic that buyers ate in the hope of a paler, clearer face. Brands such as Dr. Campbell's Safe Arsenic Complexion Wafers were advertised in newspapers to remove freckles, moles and pimples.

The appearance goal was a fashionably pale, blemish-free complexion. The product is of historical interest today as an example of how arsenic was sold as a cosmetic before modern regulation, and it is not a current option.
quick.how: Historically the wafers were taken by mouth, like a sweet or biscuit, over a course of boxes. A British advertisement of 1896 offered a full box of Mackenzie's wafers for 4s. 6d. post free [3]. Similar products were sold under other doctors' names.
quick.risks: Arsenic is toxic and cumulative. Reported harms of the period include loss of sight in one newspaper-reported case and the death of an 18-year-old in St. Louis in 1911 after several boxes [3]. Modern health agencies classify arsenic as a poison and carcinogen, and arsenic cosmetics are no longer sold.

lead: Arsenic complexion wafers were tablets marketed in the late 19th century, chiefly in the United States and Britain, to be eaten for a pale, clear complexion. Newspaper advertisements of the Victorian era promoted them as a way to remove facial blemishes such as moles and pimples [1]. The main US brand was Dr. Campbell's Safe Arsenic Wafers, which were still sold into the 1920s [3].

Their appeal rested on beauty ideals of the period, which prized pale, unblemished skin. Arsenic was also used in other cosmetic products of the era, including washes, soaps and hair dyes, and the Science Museum Group notes arsenic products continued to be sold into the 20th century [2].

chain: Claimed to clear freckles, tan and blemishes
angle.text: Advertisements claimed the wafers cleared freckles and blemishes and produced a pale complexion. The product is documented as a historical practice.

paras: The wafers were sold as an ingestible beauty aid. A 1896 London advertisement for Mackenzie's wafers promised a complexion clear and fresh, free of blemishes, redness, freckles and pimples, and the same seller offered an arsenical toilet soap also called harmless [3]. Advertisers stressed that the wafers were safe, a common approach among patent-medicine sellers of the time [2].
According to one account, the proprietor of Dr. Campbell's wafers took arsenic himself to cure a sallow complexion after yellow fever [3].

Arsenic's use for skin appearance is older than the wafers. Wikipedia notes an Elizabethan practice of applying a whitening makeup of vinegar, chalk and arsenic, with some arsenic absorbed into the bloodstream [1]. The Science Museum Group lists arsenic in 19th-century cosmetic washes, tooth cement and hair dyes, and an 18th-century hair-removal recipe using orpiment [2].

Arsenic is recognised as a poison. The wafers are described as working by destroying red blood cells so that skin looked paler, and regular small doses could build tolerance without always ending well [3]. Reported cases include a young woman who gradually lost her sight, reported in the Indianapolis Sentinel in 1880, and Hildegarde Walton, 18, of St. Louis, who died in 1911 after taking several boxes [3]. The Science Museum Group describes skin damage, blistering and organ failure from heavy arsenic exposure in other cosmetic contexts [2].
